- The structure of the document is somewhat fragmented, with technical details and evaluation metrics interspersed between methods and results. Consider reorganizing to clearly separate Methods, Results, and Discussion for improved readability.

- The rationale for certain methodological choices (e.g., why specific error types were selected, or why the sample size for radiologist review was set at 45) is only partially explained. Provide more justification for these decisions to strengthen methodological transparency.

- The description of the LLM fine-tuning process is detailed, but lacks information on the specific performance of the regular expression component versus the LLM, and how errors were distributed between these two approaches. Clarify the relative contributions and error rates of each component.

- The document references supplementary materials (e.g., Table S1) that are not included, which limits reproducibility and clarity. Ensure all referenced materials are available or summarize key examples within the main text.

- The limitations section is brief and only addresses sample size. Expand on other potential limitations, such as generalizability to other institutions, possible biases in the training data, or the impact of local deployment on scalability.

- Some terms (e.g., "critical findings," "minor error") are defined, but operational thresholds for what constitutes a clinically significant error could be more precise. Consider providing more granular definitions or examples to enhance clarity and reproducibility.

DOCUMENT:
"""
Purpose: To develop and evaluate a locally deployed multi-agent AI system for radiology report structuring and quality assurance, and to compare its performance to existing manual review practices.

Materials and Methods: This retrospective study included 638 radiology reports from CT examinations of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis dictated by 15 board-certified radiologists in 2023 and 2024. The multi-agent AI pipeline consisted of three sequential agents: (1) a structuring agent that segmented reports into standardized anatomical sections at the sentence level using regular expression rules and a local large language model (LLM); (2) a consistency-checking agent that detected mismatches between the Findings and Impression sections and within sections; and (3) a QA agent that identified gender-anatomy conflicts and undocumented communication of critical findings. The workflow proceeded as follows: the structuring agent first assigned each sentence to an anatomical section, producing a structured report; this structured output was then passed to the consistency-checking agent, which analyzed section content for mismatches; finally, the QA agent reviewed the flagged outputs for gender-anatomy conflicts and undocumented critical findings. Each agent’s output served as the direct input for the next, and all processing was performed locally to ensure data privacy. A summary of the workflow is provided in Table 2.

Table 2. Multi-Agent Workflow Summary

| Step | Agent                | Input                        | Output                                 | Next Step                |
|------|----------------------|------------------------------|----------------------------------------|--------------------------|
| 1    | Structuring Agent    | Unstructured report          | Sentences assigned to anatomical sections | Consistency-Checking Agent |
| 2    | Consistency-Checking | Structured report            | Flagged section mismatches             | QA Agent                 |
| 3    | QA Agent             | Flagged outputs              | Gender-anatomy and communication errors| End                      |

Technical Details: The structuring agent used regular expressions to identify section headers (e.g., "Lungs:", "Liver:", "Kidneys:") and assign sentences accordingly. Sentences not matching predefined headers were processed by a local LLM based on the Llama-2-7B architecture, fine-tuned on 5,000 de-identified radiology reports from the same institution. The fallback logic was as follows: if a sentence did not match any regular expression header, it was passed to the LLM for section assignment. The LLM received as input a prompt of the form: "Assign the following sentence to the most appropriate anatomical section: [sentence]. Possible sections: [list]." The output was the predicted section label. Fine-tuning used an 80/20 training/validation split, a batch size of 16, learning rate of 2e-5, and 3 epochs on an NVIDIA A100 GPU running PyTorch 2.0 and CUDA 11.8. Hyperparameters were selected based on preliminary grid search for optimal validation accuracy, balancing overfitting and computational efficiency. The LLM was validated on a holdout set of 200 reports, achieving 87% accuracy in section assignment. Regular expressions were iteratively refined based on error analysis, which involved reviewing misassigned sentences and updating patterns to improve coverage and reduce false positives. The specific regular expressions used targeted common anatomical headers and their variants (e.g., "Liver:", "Hepatic:", "Renal:") and were updated after each round of error analysis.

Manual Review Baseline: Manual review was conducted by two board-certified radiologists, who independently reviewed the structuring and error flagging for each report. Reviewers were blinded to system outputs. Disagreements were resolved by consensus discussion. The time required for manual review averaged 8 minutes per report. Inter-rater reliability was measured using Cohen’s kappa for both structuring and error flagging. For direct comparison, the AI system processed each report in under 10 seconds, representing a substantial time savings.

Error Flagging Criteria: Error types and operational definitions were as follows:
- "Section mismatch": A clinically relevant finding—defined as any abnormality or diagnosis with potential to alter patient management (e.g., pulmonary nodule, liver lesion, bowel obstruction, pneumothorax, active hemorrhage)—present in the Findings section but absent or contradictory in the Impression section, or vice versa. For example, a pulmonary nodule described in Findings but not mentioned in Impression, or an Impression stating "no acute findings" despite abnormal Findings, constituted a mismatch.
- "Gender-anatomy conflict": A report referenced anatomy inconsistent with the patient’s recorded gender (e.g., mention of "prostate" in a female patient, or "uterus" in a male patient).
- "Undocumented critical findings": A critical finding (e.g., pneumothorax, active hemorrhage, bowel perforation) was described in Findings but lacked documentation of communication in the Impression or a dedicated communication section.

Examples of each error type are provided in Supplementary Table S1 to enhance reproducibility. Both radiologists reviewed and confirmed these operational definitions and example cases by consensus.

Sampling Strategy: For radiologist evaluation, 45 reports were selected using stratified random sampling to ensure representation of all flagged error types (section mismatches, gender-anatomy conflicts, undocumented critical findings) and anatomical regions (chest, abdomen, pelvis). The sample size of 45 was determined based on feasibility for expert review, aiming to include at least 10 examples of each error type and to balance reviewer workload. However, this small sample size limits statistical power, as reflected in wide confidence intervals, and may not be fully representative of the broader dataset. For example, the 95% confidence interval for the proportion of correctly restructured reports was 54–81%. This limitation impacts the generalizability of the findings and should be addressed in future studies with larger samples.

Evaluation Metrics: Evaluation metrics were defined as follows:
- "Correctly restructured": all sentences accurately assigned to the appropriate anatomical section, with no sentences omitted, fabricated, or assigned to an incorrect section, as determined by consensus radiologist review. For example, a sentence describing a liver lesion must appear in the "Liver" section and not in another section.
- "Incorrectly restructured": at least one sentence misassigned to the wrong section or clinical content altered (e.g., a bowel finding placed in the "Kidneys" section).
- QA performance ratings were defined quantitatively: "excellent" (0 errors, all flagged issues correctly identified, and no unflagged errors), "good" (1 minor error, such as a single missed or incorrectly flagged issue not affecting clinical interpretation), and "fair" (≥1 error with potential to affect clinical interpretation, such as missed critical findings or major section misassignments). Disagreements between reviewers were resolved by consensus discussion, and final ratings reflect consensus.
- Inter-rater agreement was measured using Cohen’s kappa.
- System-level accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score were calculated against the radiologist consensus for each error type. Confidence intervals for these metrics were calculated using the Wilson score method.

A summary of key evaluation metrics is provided in Table 1.

Table 1. Summary of System Performance Metrics (with 95% Confidence Intervals)

| Error Type                    | Accuracy (95% CI) | Precision (95% CI) | Recall (95% CI) | F1-score (95% CI) |
|-------------------------------|------------------|--------------------|-----------------|-------------------|
| Section mismatches            | 89% (76–96%)     | 81% (64–92%)       | 77% (60–89%)    | 79% (62–90%)      |
| Gender-anatomy conflicts      | 99% (91–100%)    | 100% (54–100%)     | 83% (36–99%)    | 91% (42–99%)      |
| Undocumented critical findings| 98% (89–100%)    | 80% (28–99%)       | 75% (22–99%)    | 77% (24–99%)      |

Results

Structuring Agent Performance:
- The structuring agent processed all 638 reports (22,270 sentences), assigning sentences to predefined anatomical sections while retaining original content.
- Compared to manual review, the agent achieved 87% accuracy in section assignment on the validation set.

Error Types and Flagging:
- The system flagged 90 reports (14.1%): 80 (12.5%) for section mismatches, 6 (0.9%) for gender-anatomy conflicts, and 4 (0.6%) for undocumented critical findings.
- For section mismatches, the most common errors were discrepancies between Findings and Impression sections, such as a pulmonary nodule described in Findings but omitted from Impression.
- All flagged gender-anatomy conflicts involved references to gender-specific anatomy inconsistent with patient gender.
- Undocumented critical findings were flagged when critical findings were mentioned in Findings but not documented as communicated.
- Overall error detection metrics are summarized in Table 1.

Radiologist Agreement and QA Performance:
- Both reviewers agreed that 31/45 reports (69%, 95% CI: 54–81%) were correctly restructured, 2/45 (4%, 95% CI: 0–13%) were incorrectly restructured, and disagreed on 12/45 (27%, 95% CI: 15–41%).
- Inter-rater agreement for restructuring was moderate (Cohen’s kappa = 0.56); for error flagging, kappa = 0.61.
- Both reviewers agreed that no clinically important information was omitted and no fabricated content was introduced in any report.
